title: 1 Chronicles 14:8–17
context: 1 Chronicles 14:8–17 parallels 2 Samuel 5:17–25, the two Philistine attacks in the valley of Rephaim. In both accounts David inquires before each battle and receives different instructions each time. Useful differences are named rather than harmonized: Chronicles often reads God where Samuel reads the LORD; 14:12 reports that the Philistine gods were burned at David’s command, where 2 Samuel 5:21 says David and his men took the images away; and 14:16 reads Gibeon where 2 Samuel 5:25 reads Geba. The closing summary in 14:17 has no parallel in Samuel. The place name Baal Perazim is usually explained as lord who breaks out, which echoes the LORD breaking out against Uzza in 13:11. Both traditions highlight David’s dependence on God’s guidance and the LORD fighting for his people.

verses.text: When the Philistines heard that David was anointed king over all Israel, all the Philistines went up to seek David; and David heard of it, and went out against them.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the Philistines hear that David has been anointed king over all Israel, they come up to seek him, and David hears and “went out against them.” The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:17 says he “went down to the stronghold”.

Arminian readers see the unity of the nation under David drawing immediate opposition, a test of whether the new king will rely on the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the different verbs in the two accounts and let each stand without forcing them into a single sequence of movements, while reading the verse as the beginning of a test that David meets by seeking God.

Both traditions read the Philistine threat as real and David’s response as faithful, and they treat the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: Now the Philistines had come and made a raid in the valley of Rephaim.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines come and make a raid in the valley of Rephaim. The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:18 says they spread themselves in the valley.

Arminian readers see a real military danger close to Jerusalem, which sets the stage for David’s choice to inquire of God instead of relying on his own judgment, experience, or past success in war.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the valley of Rephaim is commonly located near Jerusalem, as the notes on 2 Samuel 5:18 also observe, and they read the verse as setting the scene for a battle in which God will show that he fights for his people.

Both traditions read the verse as narrative setting and as shared ground.

verses.text: David inquired of God, saying, “Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you deliver them into my hand?” The LORD said to him, “Go up; for I will deliver them into your hand.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David inquires of God whether to go up and whether God will deliver the Philistines into his hand, and the LORD answers, “Go up; for I will deliver them into your hand.” The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:19 reads “I will certainly deliver the Philistines into your hand”.

Arminian readers see David’s dependence on God as a model, with God answering a sincere request.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the promise of victory comes from God before the battle begins, and they note the contrast with Saul, of whom Chronicles says he “didn’t inquire of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 10:14).

Both traditions see David’s habit of inquiring as a mark of a godly king and read the verse as shared ground about seeking God’s guidance.

verses.text: So they came up to Baal Perazim, and David defeated them there. David said, God has broken my enemies by my hand, like waters breaking out. Therefore they called the name of that place Baal Perazim.
verses.arminianNotes:
They come up to Baal Perazim, and David defeats them there. David says, “God has broken my enemies by my hand, like waters breaking out”, and the place is named Baal Perazim. The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:20 has “The LORD has broken my enemies before me”.

Arminian readers note that the victory comes through David’s real participation, his hand, while David gives the credit to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that David’s hand is God’s instrument and that the power belongs to God, who breaks out like bursting waters. They note the echo of Perez Uzza in 13:11, where the LORD broke out against Uzza.

Both traditions affirm that God acts through human action and that the glory belongs to him, and they treat the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: They left their gods there; and David gave a command, and they were burned with fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines leave their gods there, and at David’s command they are burned with fire. The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:21 reads “They left their images there, and David and his men took them away.”

Arminian readers see the helplessness of idols that cannot even save themselves, a reversal of the time when the Philistines captured the ark (1 Samuel 4–5).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the burning agrees with the law’s command to “burn their engraved images with fire” (Deuteronomy 7:5), and they let the two accounts stand side by side without harmonizing them, as the notes on 2 Samuel 5:21 also do.

Both traditions read the verse as showing the LORD’s victory over the gods of the nations.

verses.text: The Philistines made another raid in the valley.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines make another raid in the valley. One victory does not end every threat.

Arminian readers see that past success does not remove the need for present dependence, so David must again choose to seek God rather than assume that the same approach will work a second time, and they apply this to the ongoing life of faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the repeated attack sets up the different instructions in the next verse, and they read it as a reminder that God’s people live by his continuing guidance rather than by a method that once worked.

Both traditions read the verse as teaching continued dependence on God, and they treat it as shared ground about prayer and guidance in every new situation.

verses.text: David inquired again of God; and God said to him, “You shall not go up after them. Turn away from them, and come on them opposite the mulberry trees.
verses.arminianNotes:
David inquires of God again, and God tells him not to go up after them but to “Turn away from them,” and to come at them opposite the mulberry trees. The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:23 has “Circle around behind them”.

Arminian readers see David’s humility in asking again, and God giving fresh guidance for a new situation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that God directs the strategy and not only the outcome, so that obedience means following his specific word rather than repeating what worked before. The identity of the trees is uncertain, as the notes on 2 Samuel 5:24 also say.

Both traditions read the verse as a lesson in attentive obedience and keep the two accounts’ wording as it stands.

verses.text: When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, then go out to battle; for God has gone out before you to strike the army of the Philistines.”
verses.arminianNotes:
When David hears the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, he is to go out to battle, for God has gone out before him to strike the Philistine army. The parallel is 2 Samuel 5:24.

Arminian readers see the sign as God’s assurance of his presence, calling David to act with readiness and trust at the moment God makes plain, so that divine leading and human response belong together.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the image of God marching ahead of his people as a vivid picture of the LORD fighting for Israel, so that David’s going out follows God’s prior going out.

Both traditions read the verse as stressing that the victory belongs to God, and they hold that human courage and divine action are not rivals here.

verses.text: David did as God commanded him; and they attacked the army of the Philistines from Gibeon even to Gezer.
verses.arminianNotes:
David does as God commanded him, and they strike the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer. The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:25 reads Geba where this verse reads Gibeon, and the difference is noted here rather than harmonized.

Arminian readers see obedience leading to victory, and they read the verse as the summary of a king who listens to God, in contrast with Saul.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note, as the notes on 2 Samuel 5:25 do, that the key phrase is that David did as God commanded him, showing God’s blessing on a king who obeys his word.

Both traditions treat the place names as a matter for careful study, not doctrine, and they read the verse as shared ground about obedience and the faithfulness of God.

verses.text: The fame of David went out into all lands; and the LORD brought the fear of him on all nations.
verses.arminianNotes:
The fame of David goes out into all lands, and the LORD brings the fear of him on all nations. This summary has no parallel in 2 Samuel 5.

Arminian readers note that God honors David’s faithful dependence, and they see David’s reputation serving God’s purpose among the nations, a reminder that faithfulness has real consequences in history.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that it is the LORD who brings the fear of David on the nations, so that David’s fame is God’s gift rather than his own achievement, and they see the verse as preparing for the promise of chapter 17.

Both traditions read the verse as giving glory to God for David’s success and treat it as shared ground about the LORD’s rule over the nations.
